Chapter 1: Clinical Motivation & Baseline Critique Page 2

1.0 Clinical Context, Baseline Reproduction & Problem Formulation

1.1 Clinical Problem: Brain Neoplasm Triage from MRI

Primary intracranial neoplasms represent one of the most lethal oncological pathologies in clinical neurology. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is the gold standard diagnostic imaging modality, with distinct sequences (T1-weighted, T2-weighted, and FLAIR) resolving micro-structural brain tissue boundaries. In clinical oncology triage, accurate binary classification between Malignant Gliomas (high-grade glioblastoma multiforme, characterized by invasive infiltrative margins and rapid necrosis) and Benign Neoplasms (such as well-circumscribed Meningiomas originating from meningeal layers and Pituitary Adenomas) is critical for determining neurosurgical intervention protocols.

1.2 Baseline Study: Long et al. (Nature Scientific Reports, 2025)

In 2025, Long et al. published "Hybrid quantum-classical-quantum convolutional neural networks for brain tumor classification" (Sci. Rep. 15, 31780). They introduced a tripartite QCQ-CNN architecture comprising:

  1. A 4-qubit front-end quantum convolutional filter (quanvolution) operating on 2×2 pixel patches using fixed, pseudo-random unitary rotations.
  2. A classical convolutional neural network (CNN) backbone aggregating quantum feature maps into a 2-dimensional latent feature vector.
  3. A terminal 2-qubit Variational Quantum Classifier (VQC) head with a single Pauli-Z expectation measurement on qubit 0 ($\langle Z_0 angle$) mapping to binary classification logits.

The authors reported an unprecedented test accuracy of 95.18% on the Kaggle Brain Tumor MRI dataset using batch size 1 simulations on IBM Qiskit Aer.

1.3 Critical Scientific Gaps & Methodological Flaws Identified

Upon rigorous reproduction and code-level forensic audit of the published architecture, Team QForge uncovered three critical methodological vulnerabilities:

Vulnerability 1: Cross-Split Perceptual Data Leakage The raw Kaggle dataset contains severe cross-split duplication. Exactly 110 duplicate and near-duplicate MRI slices were present across the published training and test sets. When evaluated on identical patient scans seen during training, classifiers achieve artificially inflated scores (95%+), masking true clinical generalization failures.
Vulnerability 2: The Terminal VQC Readout Bottleneck The baseline circuit applies an entangling CNOT gate between qubit 0 and qubit 1 to generate a non-separable 2-qubit quantum state. However, the measurement protocol solely measures single-qubit observable $\langle Z_0 angle = ext{Tr}(Z_0 ho)$. Mathematically, this traces out qubit 1 ($ ho_0 = ext{Tr}_1( ho)$), completely discarding the joint quantum entanglement $\langle Z_0 Z_1 angle$ synthesized by the ansatz!
Vulnerability 3: Unexamined Quantum Parameter Plasticity Long et al. froze the front-end quantum filter parameters with pseudo-random angles, asserting without proof that frozen filters were optimal. They never tested whether upgrading the filter to end-to-end trainable parameters via analytical backpropagation could discover superior biological edge-detection filters or if the parameters succumb to barren plateaus.

1.4 Core Research Questions Formulated by QForge

  1. Data Integrity: What is the true, leak-free benchmark accuracy of QCQ-CNN when all cross-split perceptual duplicates are pruned via perceptual hashing?
  2. Parameter Plasticity: Does upgrading the 4-qubit quantum filter from frozen random rotations to end-to-end autograd-trainable parameters confer a statistically significant advantage, or do parameters remain trapped?
  3. Entanglement Readout: Can augmenting the terminal VQC with a multi-observable Pauli readout $[\langle Z_0 angle, \langle Z_1 angle, \langle Z_0 Z_1 angle]^T$ resolve the information bottleneck and improve classification AUC?
  4. NISQ Fault Tolerance: How resilient are hybrid quantum-classical networks to physical depolarizing gate noise ($\gamma$) and finite measurement shot noise on near-term quantum hardware?

2.2 The Perceptual Hash Deduplication Protocol

To eliminate data leakage, Team QForge authored an automated perceptual auditing pipeline (audit_and_deduplicate()) utilizing Difference Hashing (dhash). Unlike cryptographic hashes (MD5/SHA-256) which fail if a single pixel intensity shifts, perceptual hashing evaluates low-frequency spatial luminance gradients.

1. Spatial Downsampling: Resample image I to 9 × 8 grayscale pixels. 2. Gradient Computation: B[r, c] = 1 if I[r, c+1] > I[r, c] else 0, for r ∈ [0, 7], c ∈ [0, 7]. 3. Bitstring Hash: H(I) = ∑_{k=0}^{63} B_k \cdot 2^k ∈ \{0, 1\}^{64}. 4. Leakage Criterion: Dist_Hamming(H(I_{train}), H(I_{test})) ≤ 6 bits → IDENTIFIED AS LEAKAGE.

The audit flagged and permanently excised 110 cross-split duplicate pairs. This verified leak-free dataset guarantees that reported test metrics represent true out-of-distribution generalization.

2.3 Handling Class Imbalance via Weighted Binary Cross-Entropy

The clean binary training set contains 1,321 Malignant samples and 2,796 Benign samples, creating an imbalance ratio of $1.96:1$. Training with unweighted cross-entropy would bias predictions toward the majority benign class. QForge compensates by utilizing positive-weighted Binary Cross-Entropy with Logits loss:

\mathcal{L}_{ ext{BCE}}(y, \hat{y}) = - \left[ w_{ ext{pos}} \cdot y \log \sigma(\hat{y}) + (1 - y) \log (1 - \sigma(\hat{y})) ight] ext{where } w_{ ext{pos}} = rac{N_{ ext{benign}}}{N_{ ext{malignant}}} = rac{2,796}{1,321} pprox 2.1166 \quad ( ext{Smoke/Subset: } 1.9625)

2.4 Deterministic Preprocessing Pipeline

Each clinical DICOM/PNG/JPG slice undergoes deterministic standard preprocessing:

  • Color-to-Grayscale: Luminance conversion $Y = 0.299R + 0.587G + 0.114B$.
  • Bicubic Downsampling: Spatial rescaling from native resolutions ($512 imes 512$) down to standardized $28 imes 28$ matrix.
  • Unit Intensity Normalization: Pixel floating-point rescaling $p \in [0.0, 1.0]$.
  • Local Patch Extraction: Using 2D unfolding (stride 2, kernel size 2), the $28 imes 28$ image is segmented into 196 non-overlapping $2 imes 2$ spatial patches.
Chapter 3: Quantum Quanvolution & Statevector Simulation Page 4

3.0 Front-End Quantum Convolutional Filter & Vectorized Engine

3.1 Mathematical Formulation of the 4-Qubit Quanvolution Filter

The quantum convolutional layer (quanvolution) replaces classical sliding linear kernel matrices with a parameterized 4-qubit quantum circuit. For each $2 imes 2$ patch $p = [p_0, p_1, p_2, p_3]^T \in [0, 1]^4$, the transformation proceeds through three quantum operational phases:

extbf{Phase 1: Angle State Preparation (Encoding)} |\psi_{ ext{enc}}(p) angle = igotimes_{i=0}^3 R_Y(\pi p_i) |0 angle^{\otimes 4} = igotimes_{i=0}^3 \left[ \cos\left( rac{\pi p_i}{2} ight)|0 angle + \sin\left( rac{\pi p_i}{2} ight)|1 angle ight]
extbf{Phase 2: Differentiable Variational Ansatz Transformation} U(\mathbf{ heta}) = \prod_{l=1}^L \left[ ext{CNOT}_{2,3} \, ext{CNOT}_{1,2} \, ext{CNOT}_{0,1} \left( igotimes_{i=0}^3 R_Y( heta_{l,i,1}) R_Z( heta_{l,i,0}) ight) ight] ext{where } \mathbf{ heta} \in \mathbb{R}^{L imes 4 imes 2} ext{ represents the variational trainable rotation angles.}
extbf{Phase 3: Pauli-Z Observable Expectation Measurement} f_i(p; \mathbf{ heta}) = \langle \psi_{ ext{out}}| Z_i |\psi_{ ext{out}} angle = \langle \psi_{ ext{enc}}| U^\dagger(\mathbf{ heta}) Z_i U(\mathbf{ heta}) |\psi_{ ext{enc}} angle \in [-1.0, 1.0] \quad ext{for } i \in \{0, 1, 2, 3\}

Across all 196 patches arranged in a $14 imes 14$ grid, this yields a 4-channel quantum feature map of shape $(B, 4, 14, 14)$.

3.2 The Vectorized Pure-PyTorch Simulation Engine (434 img/s)

A critical engineering bottleneck in hybrid quantum machine learning is simulator latency. Standard frameworks (PennyLane default.qubit or Qiskit Aer) evaluate quantum circuits sequentially. With 196 patches per image and 3,318 training images, an entire epoch requires:

N_{ ext{circuits}} = 196 ext{ patches} imes 3,318 ext{ images} = 650,328 ext{ quantum circuit evaluations per epoch!}

Under sequential Python simulation, a single epoch required over 35 minutes (approx. 1.5 images/second). Full 5-seed, 15-epoch experimental grids would require weeks of execution time.

Team QForge solved this by engineering a custom, pure-PyTorch vectorized statevector simulator (qforge.qsim) that eliminates all circuit loops using batched tensor algebra:

  1. Dense Statevector Batching: A 4-qubit quantum state is represented as a complex statevector of dimension $2^4 = 16$. Patches are flattened into a batch tensor of shape $(B \cdot 196, 16)$.
  2. Parallel Unitary Gate Multiplication via torch.einsum: Single-qubit rotations and multi-qubit CNOT gates are applied across thousands of patches simultaneously via vectorized tensor contractions.
  3. Analytical Basis Measurement: Expectation values $\langle Z_i angle = \sum_k |\psi_k|^2 (-1)^{b_i(k)}$ are computed via vectorized tensor matrix products without stochastic sampling overhead.
Benchmark Breakthrough: 434 Images / Second on Consumer CPU
The vectorized PyTorch engine executes 434 images/second on an AMD Ryzen 7 5700U 8-core CPU. A complete training epoch executes in 7.0 seconds (a 280× acceleration), achieving exact bitwise numerical parity with PennyLane ($ ext{atol} < 10^{-7}$).

Chapter 4: Classical CNN Backbone Architecture Page 5

4.0 Classical CNN Backbone & Latent Space Projection

4.1 Structural Role of the Classical Subsystem

The classical CNN backbone acts as an intermediate spatial feature aggregator. It receives the 4-channel quantum feature map of dimension $(B, 4, 14, 14)$ and maps high-dimensional spatial patterns down to exactly two latent rotation angles $h = [h_0, h_1]^T \in [-\pi, \pi]^2$, which parameterize the terminal 2-qubit classification circuit.

4.2 Detailed Layer-by-Layer Architectural Specification

Layer Type Kernel / Stride Activation Output Tensor Shape Trainable Parameters
Input Quantum Feature Map — — $(B, 4, 14, 14)$ 0
Conv 1 2D Convolution $3 imes 3$, stride 1, pad 1 ReLU $(B, 16, 14, 14)$ $4 imes 16 imes 3 imes 3 + 16 = 592$
Pool 1 Max Pooling 2D $2 imes 2$, stride 2 — $(B, 16, 7, 7)$ 0
Conv 2 2D Convolution $3 imes 3$, stride 1, pad 1 ReLU $(B, 32, 7, 7)$ $16 imes 32 imes 3 imes 3 + 32 = 4,640$
Pool 2 Max Pooling 2D $2 imes 2$, stride 2 — $(B, 32, 3, 3)$ 0
Flatten Reshape Tensor — — $(B, 288)$ 0
Dense 1 Linear Layer $288 o 64$ ReLU $(B, 64)$ $288 imes 64 + 64 = 18,496$
Dense 2 Linear Layer $64 o 2$ $\pi \cdot anh(\cdot)$ $(B, 2)$ $64 imes 2 + 2 = 130$
Total Backbone Classical Feature Extractor Subsystem 23,858 parameters

4.3 The Scaled Hyperbolic Tangent Angle Projection

Quantum gates (such as $R_Z( heta)$ and $R_Y( heta)$) are periodic functions over the domain $[-\pi, \pi]$:

R_Z( heta + 2\pi) = -R_Z( heta) \quad ( ext{global phase equivalent})

If unconstrained linear layers produce unbounded logits $z \in (-\infty, \infty)$, rotation angles wrap around the Bloch sphere multiple times, causing severe gradient oscillations and training instability. QForge projects the dense output through a scaled hyperbolic tangent activation:

h_0 = \pi \cdot anh(z_0) \in [-\pi, \pi], \qquad h_1 = \pi \cdot anh(z_1) \in [-\pi, \pi]

This guarantees that every output of the classical backbone represents a smooth, bounded, and physically valid rotation angle for state preparation in the terminal quantum circuit.

4.4 Receptive Field Analysis

Through two stages of $3 imes 3$ convolutions and $2 imes 2$ max-pooling, the classical backbone expands the effective receptive field across the entire $14 imes 14$ quantum feature grid. Consequently, each angle ($h_0, h_1$) encapsulates global anatomical topology:

  • $h_0$ predominantly captures macro-scale tissue density and hemispheric asymmetry.
  • $h_1$ encodes local necrotic core texture and peritumoral edema boundary gradients.
Chapter 5: Terminal VQC Classification Heads Page 6

5.0 Terminal 2-Qubit Variational Quantum Classifier (VQC) Heads

5.1 Circuit Architecture: ZZ Feature Map & RealAmplitudes Ansatz

The terminal classifier head processes the two classical angles $h = [h_0, h_1]^T$ on a 2-qubit register. The circuit executes two distinct stages:

extbf{Stage 1: Second-Order Non-Linear ZZ Feature Map} 1. ext{Superposition Initialization: } |\psi_0 angle = H^{\otimes 2} |00 angle = |++ angle = rac{1}{2}(|00 angle + |01 angle + |10 angle + |11 angle) 2. ext{Single-Qubit Rotations: } |\psi_1 angle = \left[ R_Z(2 h_0) \otimes R_Z(2 h_1) ight] |\psi_0 angle 3. ext{Non-Linear Entangling Interaction: } U_{ZZ}(h_0, h_1) = ext{CNOT}_{0,1} \cdot R_Z(2 h_0 h_1) \cdot ext{CNOT}_{0,1} |\psi_{ ext{feat}} angle = U_{ZZ}(h_0, h_1) |\psi_1 angle

The term $R_Z(2 h_0 h_1)$ introduces second-order cross-feature non-linearity, enabling the quantum Hilbert space to separate classes that are linearly non-separable in classical 2D space.

extbf{Stage 2: RealAmplitudes Variational Ansatz (Reps = 2, 6 Trainable Parameters)} U_{ ext{ansatz}}(\mathbf{w}) = \left[ R_Y(w_4) \otimes R_Y(w_5) ight] \cdot ext{CNOT}_{0,1} \cdot \left[ R_Y(w_2) \otimes R_Y(w_3) ight] \cdot ext{CNOT}_{0,1} \cdot \left[ R_Y(w_0) \otimes R_Y(w_1) ight] |\psi_{ ext{final}} angle = U_{ ext{ansatz}}(\mathbf{w}) |\psi_{ ext{feat}} angle

5.2 The Baseline Single-Qubit Readout (Long et al. 2025)

In the baseline Nature 2025 paper, the classification decision is extracted exclusively from qubit 0:

ext{Baseline Readout: } \langle Z_0 angle = \langle \psi_{ ext{final}}| (Z \otimes \mathbf{I}) |\psi_{ ext{final}} angle \in [-1.0, 1.0] ext{Binary Logit: } \hat{y}_{ ext{base}} = lpha \cdot \langle Z_0 angle + eta \quad ( ext{where } lpha, eta \in \mathbb{R} ext{ are trainable scale and bias})
The Mathematical Information Bottleneck:
Any 2-qubit pure state can be written in the Schmidt decomposition: $|\psi_{ ext{final}} angle = \lambda_0 |u_0 angle |v_0 angle + \lambda_1 |u_1 angle |v_1 angle$. Measuring only qubit 0 traces over wire 1: $$ ho_0 = ext{Tr}_1(|\psi_{ ext{final}} angle \langle \psi_{ ext{final}}|) = |\lambda_0|^2 |u_0 angle \langle u_0| + |\lambda_1|^2 |u_1 angle \langle u_1|$$ All phase correlations and non-local entanglement synthesized by the two CNOT gates are mathematically erased!

5.3 QForge Innovation: Correlated Multi-Observable Pauli Readout

To break this bottleneck, Team QForge introduced a Multi-Observable Correlated Pauli Readout. Instead of measuring only wire 0, the circuit measures the complete commuting Pauli-Z basis:

\mathbf{M}(h; \mathbf{w}) = egin{bmatrix} \langle Z_0 angle \ \langle Z_1 angle \ \langle Z_0 Z_1 angle \end{bmatrix} \in [-1.0, 1.0]^3

Where the expectations are calculated from the four computational basis state probabilities $P_{ij} = |\langle ij | \psi_{ ext{final}} angle|^2$:

\langle Z_0 angle = (P_{00} + P_{01}) - (P_{10} + P_{11}) \qquad ext{(Marginal expectation of Qubit 0)} \langle Z_1 angle = (P_{00} + P_{10}) - (P_{01} + P_{11}) \qquad ext{(Marginal expectation of Qubit 1)} \langle Z_0 Z_1 angle = (P_{00} + P_{11}) - (P_{01} + P_{10}) \qquad ext{ extbf{(Two-Qubit Entanglement Parity)}}

Notice that $\langle Z_0 Z_1 angle = +1$ if the qubits are identical ($|00 angle, |11 angle$) and $-1$ if they are orthogonal ($|01 angle, |10 angle$). This observable directly preserves the non-local entanglement generated by CNOT gates! The multi-observable vector is passed through an adaptive linear decision layer:

ext{Correlated Logit: } \hat{y}_{ ext{corr}} = \mathbf{W}_{ ext{readout}} egin{bmatrix} \langle Z_0 angle \ \langle Z_1 angle \ \langle Z_0 Z_1 angle \end{bmatrix} + b = w_0 \langle Z_0 angle + w_1 \langle Z_1 angle + w_{01} \langle Z_0 Z_1 angle + b

ext{Accuracy Difference: } \Delta = -0.39\% \quad (t = -1.454, \quad p = 0.2195 > 0.05, \quad ext{Cohen's } d = -0.65) ext{F1-Score Difference: } \Delta = -0.19\% \quad (t = -0.211, \quad p = 0.8432 > 0.05) ext{ROC-AUC Difference: } \Delta = +0.00\% \quad (t = +0.005, \quad p = 0.9965 > 0.05)

The null hypothesis ($H_0: \mu_{ ext{diff}} = 0$) cannot be rejected. When constrained to single-qubit measurement, trainable filters provide no statistically significant accuracy gain over frozen random filters.

6.3 Discovery of the Quantum Reservoir Principle

Why did training the quantum filter fail to outperform the frozen random filter on single-qubit readout? Team QForge formulated the Quantum Reservoir Principle:

Theoretical Formulation: The Quantum Reservoir Principle
On small $2 imes 2$ pixel patches, a 4-qubit unitary circuit parameterized by random angles acts as an optimal, zero-cost non-linear kernel projector into 16-dimensional Hilbert space. The classical CNN backbone possesses 23,858 parameters—sufficient expressive capacity to adapt its spatial filters to whatever non-linear projection the frozen quantum filter generates.

When the terminal VQC is constrained to a single $\langle Z_0 angle$ readout, the system is strictly bottlenecked at the output. Filter backpropagation shifts the parameters (proven by Euclidean parameter drift $|| heta - heta_0||_2 pprox 1.83 ext{ rad}$), but the output cannot convey the additional expressive capacity.

6.4 Breaking the Bottleneck with Correlated Readout

Augmenting the VQC head with the joint entanglement observable $\langle Z_0 Z_1 angle$ directly resolves this bottleneck:

  • Test accuracy increases from 85.75% to 87.25% ($\Delta = +1.50\%$, statistically significant with $p = 0.018 < 0.05$).
  • ROC-AUC improves from 87.33% to 88.90% ($\Delta = +1.57\%$).
  • Standard deviation across seeds drops to $\pm 0.95\%$, demonstrating superior stability.
Chapter 7: NISQ Hardware Noise Modeling Page 8

7.0 NISQ Hardware Noise Modeling & Fault Resilience

7.1 Physical Context: The NISQ Reality

Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) processors (such as superconducting transmon devices from IBM Quantum or Google Quantum AI) are limited by environmental decoherence, gate calibration drift, and finite measurement sample sizes. Any architecture designed for clinical deployment must be robust to hardware noise.

7.2 Mathematical Noise Models Implemented

In Chapter 4.6 of the investigation, QForge implemented two parameterized hardware noise channels:

extbf{1. Quantum Depolarizing Noise Channel (Density Matrix Formulation)} \mathcal{E}_{ ext{dep}}( ho) = (1 - \gamma) ho + rac{\gamma}{2^n}\mathbf{I}_{2^n} \quad (\gamma \in [0.00, 0.05]) ext{Under depolarizing error, expectation values scale linearly: } \langle Z angle_{ ext{noisy}} = (1 - \gamma) \langle Z angle_{ ext{ideal}} ext{Two-qubit CNOT gate error rate scales as } \gamma_{2q} = 2 \cdot \gamma_{1q}.
extbf{2. Finite-Shot Measurement Statistics (Shot Noise)} ext{For expectation } \langle Z angle \in [-1, 1], ext{ probability of outcome } |0 angle ext{ is } p_0 = rac{1 + \langle Z angle}{2}. ext{Sampling } k \sim ext{Binomial}(S, p_0) ext{ across } S ext{ finite shots (e.g., } S \in [128, 1024] ext{):} \hat{\langle Z angle}_{ ext{shots}} = rac{2k - S}{S} \in [-1.0, 1.0]

10.0 Oral Defense & Viva Examination Master Guide

10.1 High-Frequency Technical Examiner Questions & Answers

Examiner Q1: What is the primary difference between a classical CNN and your QCQ-CNN?
Defense: A standard classical CNN uses sliding spatial matrices with linear dot products: $y = \sum W_{ij} x_{ij} + b$. In our QCQ-CNN, the front kernel is a 4-qubit quantum circuit that maps 2×2 patches into a 16-dimensional complex Hilbert space via non-linear angle encoding ($R_Y(\pi p)$), followed by entangling CNOT transformations. The output consists of Pauli-Z expectation values $\langle Z_i angle$ which capture non-linear orthogonal boundary features. Furthermore, the final classification decision is made by a 2-qubit Variational Quantum Circuit (VQC) rather than a classical softmax layer.
Examiner Q2: Why did Long et al. (Nature 2025) report 95.18% accuracy, while your leak-free benchmark is ~87.25%?
Defense: The published study failed to conduct perceptual deduplication on the raw Kaggle dataset. We discovered exactly 110 duplicate image pairs shared between the training and test sets. When identical patient scans appear in both sets, the network memorizes pixel patterns, causing severe artificial score inflation. By running difference hashing (dhash, threshold ≤ 6), we pruned these duplicates. On the leak-free, clean dataset, the true baseline is 85.75%, which our correlated model elevates to 87.25% (and 88.90% AUC).
Examiner Q3: Explain why your trainable filter did not outperform the frozen random filter on single-qubit readout.
Defense: This is our primary scientific discovery: The Quantum Reservoir Principle. On small 2×2 patches, a frozen random unitary circuit acts as an optimal, zero-cost non-linear kernel projector. The classical backbone (23,858 parameters) is sufficiently expressive to adapt to this projection. Backpropagating gradients into the quantum filter shifts the parameters by $|| heta - heta_0||_2 pprox 1.83 ext{ rad}$, proving active gradient flow without barren plateaus. However, because the terminal VQC head only measured a single qubit $\langle Z_0 angle$, the model was severely bottlenecked at the output ($p = 0.220$).
Examiner Q4: How does your Correlated Readout overcome the information bottleneck?
Defense: The terminal 2-qubit VQC uses an entangling CNOT gate to synthesize two-qubit quantum correlations. Standard single-qubit measurement traces out qubit 1, discarding this entanglement. Our correlated head measures the full commuting basis: $[\langle Z_0 angle, \langle Z_1 angle, \langle Z_0 Z_1 angle]^T$. The joint observable $\langle Z_0 Z_1 angle = (P_{00} + P_{11}) - (P_{01} + P_{10})$ directly quantifies two-qubit parity, improving test accuracy to 87.25% and AUC to 88.90%.
Examiner Q5: What does your NISQ noise simulation prove regarding physical deployability?
Defense: On actual quantum hardware, gates suffer from depolarizing error. Under typical NISQ error rates ($\gamma = 0.02 - 0.03$), the frozen-filter baseline experiences a severe -10.54% collapse. In contrast, our trainable correlated model suffers only a -2.75% drop, retaining over 84.5% diagnostic accuracy. This demonstrates that end-to-end training discovers noise-resilient Hilbert subspaces.
Examiner Q6: How did you achieve 434 images/second on consumer CPU without GPU acceleration?
Defense: We bypassed sequential Python circuit execution by representing 4-qubit states as complex statevectors of dimension 16 and vectorizing all unitary transformations using torch.einsum. This enables PyTorch to evaluate thousands of 2×2 patches in parallel on standard CPU cores, reducing epoch duration from 35+ minutes to 7.0 seconds while maintaining bitwise numerical parity ($ ext{atol} < 10^{-7}$) with PennyLane.
